solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

definitions.meaning: to seem, to strike others a certain way

explanation.surface: A lamp or screen flickering into view as it is switched on.
explanation.walkthrough: "Light on" reads as a lamp switched on, but here it is the verb phrase to light on, meaning to happen upon something.
explanation.definitionFit: To come across is both to seem a certain way and to find something by chance.

parts.note: coy means shy
pee is how the letter P is spelt out

explanation.surface: A bashful patient handing over a urine sample at the doctor's.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a medical sample; "pee" is just the name of the letter P, and the specimen is one copy of a book or magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A copy is a single example of a printed work, so a specimen of it.

indicators.note: in a down answer, rising means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: rum means odd or suspect; turned upward it gives MUR
rain is precipitation

explanation.surface: Suspicious weather suspected of spreading illness.
explanation.walkthrough: "Suspect" looks like a verb, but it is the adjective: RUM is British slang for odd or dubious.
explanation.definitionFit: Murrain is an old word for an infectious disease of cattle, or a plague.

clue.text: Mountain I learn much about crossing area, like K2

indicators.note: the letters of I LEARN MUCH are moved about

parts.note: an alp is a mountain

indicators.note: the jumbled letters cross, or take in, the A for area

parts.note: anagram fodder
a is short for area

explanation.surface: A climber learning a lot as they cross terrain on the world's second-highest peak.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all mountaineering, so K2 reads as the peak; the definition wants it as a label made of a letter and a number.
explanation.definitionFit: K2 mixes a letter and a digit, which is what alphanumerical means.

parts.note: a rat is a wretch, a contemptible person
w is short for with; it is taken away

explanation.surface: A rat scurrying off beside the family cat.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cat" is not the animal: in British slang to cat is to vomit, so it is the verb that matches RETCH.
explanation.definitionFit: To cat is slang for to be sick, and to retch is to heave as if vomiting.

clue.text: Number and name hidden in lawgiver's calls

parts.note: a sum is a number
Moses brought down the Ten Commandments
n is short for name

explanation.surface: A number and a name tucked away in the pronouncements of an ancient lawgiver.
explanation.walkthrough: The lawgiver of the Old Testament is Moses; the 's joins him to the calls, so it is only surface grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: Summonses are official calls to appear, as before a court.

parts.note: i is short for island
bis is Latin for twice, used in music for a repeat

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher spotting the same bird twice on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: BIS is the musical instruction to play a passage twice.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibis is a long-legged wading bird with a down-curved bill.

clue.text: Short gap opens behind one sports car

parts.note: a butt is a behind
gap without its last letter
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A small gap opening up behind a racing car on the track.
explanation.walkthrough: "Behind" looks like a position in the race; it is a noun, the backside, giving BUTT.
explanation.definitionFit: Bugatti is a maker of luxury sports cars.

clue.text: Always cold in office? Leave at home

indicators.note: read as placed within: the words for always and cold end up inside the word for office

parts.note: a station is a post or office one holds
ay is an old word for always
c is short for cold

explanation.surface: A chilly office where it is always cold, so staff might as well stay home.
explanation.walkthrough: "Leave" looks like an instruction to go, but it is the noun: time off work, spent at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A staycation is a holiday taken at home rather than away.

clue.text: Unfinished food in grass on blanket

parts.note: to grass on someone is to inform on them
a dish of food, missing its last letter

explanation.surface: Half-eaten food left in the grass on a picnic blanket.
explanation.walkthrough: The picnic picture makes grass and blanket nouns; grass on is British slang for informing, and blanket is an adjective meaning all-covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A blanket ban applies to everything without distinction, which is indiscriminate.

indicators.note: something installed is fitted inside, as the mirror word is fitted into the section

parts.note: a part is a section
to ape is to mirror, to copy

explanation.surface: A builder fitting a mirror into a section of wall.
explanation.walkthrough: "Mirror" wants to be the object; it is the verb, to copy, giving APE.
explanation.definitionFit: A parapet is a low protective wall along a roof, bridge or balcony.

parts.note: the Isle of Man

indicators.note: take the middle four letters of Paraguayan

parts.note: the middle of pAR(AGUA)YAN

explanation.surface: A question about the heart of Paraguay's capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to Asunción, Paraguay's capital; the answer is the capital of Nicaragua instead. The Isle of Man is a British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the city is Nicaragua's seat of government, not Paraguay's.

clue.text: Account about Corinthians running out of time

indicators.note: the letters of Corinthians run loose into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
ac is short for account

explanation.surface: A story of the Corinthians, a football side perhaps, running out the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: "Running out of time" reads as one phrase; the anagram indicator is just "running", and "out of time" is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something anachronistic belongs to another period, so it is out of its time.

parts.note: short pastry is crisp and crumbly
gravy and bread are both slang for money

explanation.surface: Gravy poured under a crisp biscuit, an odd dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Gravy here is slang for easy money, and bread is slang for money too.
explanation.definitionFit: Shortbread is a rich, crumbly Scottish butter biscuit.

indicators.note: the answer is made of letters from the words that follow

parts.note: ganesH INDUbitably

explanation.surface: A remark that a devotee of Ganesh is surely of one faith.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: the answer spans the join between Ganesh and indubitably.
explanation.definitionFit: Ganesh, the elephant-headed god of luck and new beginnings, is a Hindu deity, so his worshipper is a Hindu.

clue.text: Deviant in Russian port piercing nuts

parts.note: mast is the nuts of forest trees such as beech and oak, fed to pigs
Sochi is a Russian Black Sea resort

explanation.surface: A pervert in a Russian port having his nuts pierced.
explanation.walkthrough: "Nuts" pulls toward crazy; it is the noun mast, the fallen nuts of beech and oak.
explanation.definitionFit: A masochist takes pleasure in pain, a deviant appetite.

parts.note: mono is the Greek-derived prefix for single or one
a thing, as in having a thing about something, is an obsession

explanation.walkthrough: Three words read as a plain object; the whole clue is also the definition, since one fixation is exactly what the word means.
explanation.definitionFit: Monomania is an obsessive preoccupation with one subject.

indicators.note: the letters are perhaps what the answer is, rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Cowards who secretly fled.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface gives cowards running away, which is what recreants do.
explanation.definitionFit: A recreant is a cowardly deserter or traitor.

clue.text: Dolphins have to get by on herring food

parts.note: to cope is to get by
a pod is a group of dolphins

explanation.surface: Dolphins needing to scrape by on a diet of herring.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes herring the dolphins' meal; the definition is what the herring eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Copepods are tiny crustaceans in plankton, a staple food of herring.

parts.note: to be into something is to be keen on it
r is short for runs in cricket

explanation.surface: An opening batsman eager to grab some runs.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes Opener a batsman; it is the opening part of a song or speech.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro is the opening section of a piece of music or a talk.

clue.text: One using X now affected by brief name

indicators.note: term is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: twee means affectedly quaint
a term is a name; brief drops its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone whose use of X is coloured by a short name or handle.
explanation.walkthrough: X is the social network formerly called Twitter, whose posts were tweets; "now" flags that X is its current name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweeter posts on Twitter, the platform now named X.

clue.text: Immersion heating that's tough to start?

definitions.text: Immersion heating that's tough to start?

parts.note: not the household water heater but a dipping in water, as in a religious rite of entry
heat as in flames, and a start that is hard going: a trying first experience

explanation.walkthrough: An immersion heater is a household water heater, so the surface is plumbing; immersion is also baptism, and heating is fire, giving a tough initiation.
explanation.definitionFit: A baptism of fire is a hard first experience of something new.

parts.note: a flight of steps
l is short for large; it is removed

explanation.surface: Stepping out of a large cardboard box.
explanation.walkthrough: "Box" is a verb here, to fight with fists, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: boxers trade punches, which is a fight.

parts.note: a bra is a support garment
d is short for died

explanation.surface: The prop behind a Pitt, whether PM or actor, has died.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possessive; it is "is", joining the definition to the wordplay. The surface hints at William Pitt, the British prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Brad is the first name of the actor Brad Pitt.

parts.note: ex means former, old
a plain is flat land

explanation.surface: Someone justifying why they left an old apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: "Flat" reads as a British apartment, but it means level ground, a plain.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: giving the reasons behind something makes it clear.

clue.text: One who really works as a joiner

definitions.meaning: graft is British slang for hard work
one who grafts, joining plant tissue or skin

explanation.surface: A carpenter praised as a genuinely hard worker.
explanation.walkthrough: Joiner suggests a carpenter; here it is literal, someone who joins by grafting.
explanation.definitionFit: A grafter is both a hard worker and one who grafts things together.

clue.text: Ranch guest right to steal diamonds

parts.note: your due is what you have a right to
d is short for diamonds in card games

explanation.surface: A guest at a ranch who feels entitled to pocket some diamonds.
explanation.walkthrough: A dude ranch is a US holiday ranch for city visitors, who are the dudes.
explanation.definitionFit: A dude is a city dweller holidaying on a western ranch.

clue.text: Neat barrier used in a minor way

definitions.text: Neat barrier used in a minor way

parts.note: not a tidy fence: neat is an old word for cows and oxen, so a barrier against them
not modestly used: a way is a road, and these sit in small country lanes

explanation.walkthrough: Neat is an old word for cattle, not tidy; a way is a road, and cattle grids sit on minor country roads.
explanation.definitionFit: A cattle grid is a set of bars over a pit in a road that livestock will not cross.
